name: Jump Squat
tierNote: Safety tier A from content.md appendix B (explosive). census.json difficulty tier 2.
parentNote: Supervisor's LB4A brief names box_jump (claude/libht-research-legs-core) as the template parent. Same hand archetype (none) and primary contact (standing-feet). content.md appendix A had jump_squat parenting box_jump; box_jump was written first, so the direction is reversed.

inherit.field: plate.frames (airborne convention: take-off and landing frames only)
inherit.why: true for this child because architecture section 1 lists the jump squat under the airborne convention.

claims.text: Stand with feet hip width, arms by the sides, shoulders down and back, trunk braced.

quotes.text: Stand with your feet feet hip-width apart, arms by your sides, depressing and retracting your scapulae (pull shoulders down and back) without arching your low back, and "brace" (engage your abdominal / core muscles) to stiffen your spine.

claims.text: Lower by moving the hips back then down, until the heels are about to lift, keeping the back flat.

quotes.text: Try to maintain a flat back by bending forward at the hips

Begin your downward phase by first shifting your hips backwards then slowly moving downwards to create a hinge-like movement at your knees. Continue to lower yourself until your feel your heels about to lift off the floor.

claims.text: After only a brief pause at the bottom, jump by extending ankles, knees and hips together.

quotes.text: With ONLY a very brief pause at the bottom of your downward phase, explode upwards through your lower extremity, achieving triple extension (pushing and extending your ankles, knees and hips simultaneously).

claims.text: Land softly and quietly on the mid-foot, rolling back to the heels, and push the hips back and down to absorb the landing.

quotes.text: Attempt to land softly and quietly on the mid-foot, rolling backwards quickly towards the heels. Always push your hips backwards and drop them downwards to absorb the impacting forces associated with jumping.

claims.text: Do not land with locked knees; ACE says it may lead to knee injury.

quotes.text: Avoid locking out your knees or quads on your landing as this may lead to potential knee injuries

claims.text: On landing, foot position matters most, and the knees should not shoot far forward, which adds knee stress.

quotes.text: The most important components of the landing phase are correct foot position and avoiding excessive forward movement in your lower extremity which places additional stresses upon your knees.

claims.text: Load progression: learn to squat and land first, start with small jumps, and jump more explosively only once landings are good.

quotes.text: It is suggested, you first learn how to squat and land before attempting to jump. Once you have mastered the hip-hinge mechanism, begin with small jumps, but emphasize your landing mechanics. Only progress to more explosive jumps once you have mastered your landing mechanics.

claims.text: Land with the trunk tipped slightly forward, head in line, back flat and the core braced.

quotes.text: Land with your trunk inclined slightly forward, head aligned with your spine and back rigid or flat.
Keep your abdominal / core muscles engaged, stiffening your torso to protect your spine.

claims.text: Squat down with control, rebound straight into a maximal vertical jump, absorb the landing by bending knees and hips; 3-5 reps per set.

quotes.text: Squat with control of proper posture and balance into the bottom, then immediately rebound up and drive into a maximal vertical jump.
Absorb the landing in a strong stance by bending the knees and hips.
Squat vertical jumps should generally be done for 3-5 reps per set, with 3-10 sets.

claims.text: Holding the hands loosely at the chest (no arm swing) puts more of the work on the legs.

quotes.text: Focus and demand on the legs can be increased by removing the swinging of the arms—hold the hands loosely at the chest.

claims.text: In drop landings, stiff landings (less knee bend) had higher ground forces, and soft landings shared the impact across the hip and knee muscles.

quotes.text: The stiff landing had larger GRFs
The hip and knee muscles absorbed more energy in the soft landing

claims.text: Quieter landings had lower vertical ground force, through more ankle and knee bend (single-leg drop landings, n=26).

quotes.text: As landing sound decreases, so does vGRF during a drop-landing task. These reductions were achieved by increasing ankle and knee joint excursions.

claims.text: ACE lists the target areas as the butt and hips and the thighs.

quotes.text: Butt/Hips, Legs - Thighs

claims.text: NHS knee pain: get advice from 111 if the knee is very painful, or locks, gives way or painfully clicks.

quotes.text: your knee is very painful
your knee locks, gives way or painfully clicks – painless clicking is normal

claims.text: Never jump to failure: fatigue spoils landing mechanics and raises injury risk. NASM says this of plyometrics as a class on its box jump page; applied to the jump squat by inference (copied from the box_jump card, c11).

quotes.text: Never perform to failure with plyometrics, as fatigue significantly compromises landing mechanics and increases injury risk.

claims.text: In 205 female athletes measured in a jump-landing task, knee motion and loading at landing, including the knee caving inward (dynamic valgus), predicted later knee ligament injury. Applied to jump-squat landings by inference (different task and population).

quotes.text: Knee motion and knee loading during a landing task are predictors of anterior cruciate ligament injury risk in female athletes.
Female athletes with increased dynamic valgus and high abduction loads are at increased risk of anterior cruciate ligament injury.

claims.text: The calves are inferred to work from the ankle extension in the take-off; no EMG source for the jump squat was read.

quotes.text: achieving triple extension (pushing and extending your ankles, knees and hips simultaneously)

plate.viewWhy: Hips-back loading (j2), triple extension (j3) and the landing knee and hip bend (j4, j5) are sagittal.
plate.frames: Airborne convention (architecture section 1): take-off and landing frames only, no mid-air pose.
plate.start: Take-off frame: bottom of the squat, hips back, heels just about to lift, back flat (j2), about to extend ankles, knees and hips (j3).
plate.end: Landing frame: on the mid-foot rolling to the heels, hips pushed back and down, knees bent (j4), trunk tipped slightly forward, back flat (j8).

checkpoints.label: Hips back
checkpoints.what: Load by sending the hips back, then down.

checkpoints.label: Full extension
checkpoints.what: Ankles, knees and hips extend together to jump.

checkpoints.label: Soft landing
checkpoints.what: Landing checkpoint: land quietly on the mid-foot, hips back and down, knees bent.

mistake.why: ACE warns locked-knee landings may lead to knee injury (j5); stiff landings raise ground forces (j11).
mistake.rankNote: ACE does not rank faults; this is the one it warns about by name. Knees shooting far forward on landing (j6) is also drawable but has no threshold to draw.

tells.text: Hips drop back as you land

tempo.text: Controlled squat down, only a brief pause, explosive jump; 3-5 reps per set, never to failure (j15). Airborne plate: take-off and landing frames only.

grip.note: Hand archetype none. Arms by the sides (j1) or hands loosely at the chest (j10).

setup.step: Learn to squat and land before jumping; start with small jumps.
Feet hip width, arms by the sides, brace.
Hips back then down until the heels are about to lift.
Brief pause, then jump with full extension.
Land quietly on the mid-foot, hips back and down.

posture.point: Back flat on the way down.
Ankles, knees and hips extend together.
Land on the mid-foot, rolling to the heels.
Knees bent on landing, never locked.
Trunk slightly forward, head in line on landing.
Knees do not cave inward on landing.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Jumping big before landings are solid.
handlingMistakes.fix: Go back to small jumps until the landing is quiet and controlled.
Land quietly, hips back, knees bending.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Knees shooting far forward on landing.
handlingMistakes.fix: Push the hips back as you land.

rows.means: Landing stiff, or knees going far forward.
rows.fix: Land softer with the hips back; make the jumps smaller.

rows.where: Very painful knee, or the knee locks or gives way

risks.risk: Knees travelling far forward on landing add knee stress.

zooms.right: Mid-foot landing, hips back and down, knees bent.
Ankles, knees and hips fully extended together.
zooms.wrong: Jumping with the hips still bent.

libraryDiff.why: Library: quads primary, glutes and calves secondary. ACE's target list covers thighs and hips (j13, WEAK); ankle extension in the take-off supports calves by inference (j17, MECH). No EMG source for the bodyweight jump squat was read. No change.

loadProgression.text: Squat and landing first, then small jumps, then more explosive ones as landings allow.

wayOut.text: Never jump to failure: end the set before fatigue spoils your landings. Only jump more explosively once your landings are mastered.

anchorNote: ACE squat jumps page read in full; Catalyst Athletics squat vertical jump page also read in full.
unsourced: An EMG source for which muscles work most in the jump squat.
Knee tracking on landing: only a jump-landing study in female athletes (j16, MECH/WEAK) was found; no jump-squat-specific source read.
Ankle red-flag row: box_jump's ankle box now comes from the NHS ankle pain page (box_jump c14; nhs-sprains was dropped there, F21); not re-read here, so not linked. (W1 lows round 2026-10-03)
